# Bones: strength and stiffness (auto-generated by `python -m rnd.run_all`)

Arm straight out horizontally with 1.0 kg (the worst static case), loads ×1.5 for dynamics. Printed PETG: E ≈ 1.8 GPa, allowable 12 MPa (layer adhesion ×0.5, safety 2). Deflection is from bone bending only (belt and bearing compliance are not included yet).

| Wall | Peak stress per segment (MPa) | Hand deflection, static |
|---|---|---|
| 2.4 mm printed | roll link (pitch → yaw): 1.0; upper-arm neck Ø72 printed: 2.0; elbow housing 98×108: 0.4; forearm side link 22×56 printed: 2.3 ✅ | 3.44 mm ⚠️ |
| 1.6 mm printed | roll link (pitch → yaw): 1.2; upper-arm neck Ø72 printed: 2.9; elbow housing 98×108: 0.7; forearm side link 22×56 printed: 3.3 ✅ | 4.79 mm ⚠️ |
| 1.2 mm printed | roll link (pitch → yaw): 1.2; upper-arm neck Ø72 printed: 3.8; elbow housing 98×108: 0.9; forearm side link 22×56 printed: 4.2 ✅ | 6.03 mm ⚠️ |
| 1.6 mm printed + **CF tubes** | roll link (pitch → yaw): 1.2; upper-arm neck CF Ø40×1: 15.2; elbow housing 98×108: 0.7; forearm CF Ø30×1: 16.7 ✅ | 1.81 mm ✅ |
| 1.2 mm printed + **CF tubes** | roll link (pitch → yaw): 1.2; upper-arm neck CF Ø40×1: 15.2; elbow housing 98×108: 0.9; forearm CF Ø30×1: 16.7 ✅ | 1.87 mm ✅ |

**Reading:** printed shells are strong enough at any practical wall thickness, but **stiffness** limits them: even 2.4 mm walls let the hand sag ~3 mm. Thinner walls save mass but make it worse. Carbon tubes for the two slender sections (precedent: Hello Robot Stretch's carbon-tube arm, Kinova's carbon links) are ~40× stiffer per section than printed PETG, and they're lighter.
Belt stretch and bearing play add further compliance; that goes in twin v1 (dynamic).
